## {data-menu-title="Learning Objectives"}

[Learning Objectives]{.slide-title}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
By the end of this lecture, students will be able to:

- define Augmented Reality (AR) and Virtual Reality (VR);
- distinguish AR, VR, and Mixed Reality (MR);
- identify the hardware and software components of AR/VR systems;
- explain the main features of AR and VR;
- describe major application areas of AR and VR;
- state the limitations and challenges of AR/VR technologies.
:::

## {data-menu-title="Think About It"}

[Think About It]{.slide-title}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- How does a phone camera show a virtual cartoon character standing on your table?
- Can you "visit" a museum, a surgery room, or a mountain without leaving the classroom?
- Why do pilots practice in flight simulators before flying real aircraft?
- Is a 360-degree video on a normal screen the same as being inside a virtual world?
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Why Reality Technologies?"}

[Why Do We Need Reality Technologies?]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- Traditional screens present information on a **flat, separate display**.
- Many tasks are naturally **three-dimensional and spatial**: surgery, construction, design, navigation, training.
- Some situations are **costly, dangerous, or impossible** to practice in the real world.
- AR and VR bring digital content closer to **human perception and interaction**.
- They are major parts of the broader idea of **immersive computing** or **extended reality (XR)**.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Reality-Virtuality Continuum"}

[The Reality-Virtuality Continuum]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    R[Real Environment] --> AR[Augmented Reality]
    AR --> AV[Augmented Virtuality]
    AV --> VR[Virtual Environment]
    subgraph MR[Mixed Reality]
      AR
      AV
    end
```

::: {.body-text-m}
- The continuum runs from the **fully real** world to a **fully virtual** world.
- **Extended Reality (XR)** is an umbrella term covering AR, VR, and MR.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="What Is Augmented Reality?"}

[What Is Augmented Reality (AR)?]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
**Augmented Reality** is a technology that **overlays computer-generated content** such as text, images, 3D models, or audio onto the user's view of the **real world** in real time.

- The user remains **in the real environment**.
- Digital content is **aligned** with real objects and locations.
- The system works **interactively and in real time**.
- AR can be experienced through smartphones, tablets, smart glasses, or head-up displays.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="How AR Works"}

[How Does AR Work?]{.slide-title}

<hr>

::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[Camera and Sensors] --> B[Tracking and Scene Understanding]
    B --> C[Registration: Align Virtual with Real]
    D[Digital Content] --> C
    C --> E[Rendering]
    E --> F[Display: Phone / Glasses]
    F -. Feedback .-> A
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.incremental .body-text-m}
- **Capture:** camera and sensors observe the surroundings.
- **Track:** the system detects surfaces, markers, or objects and estimates device position.
- **Register:** virtual content is aligned with the real scene.
- **Render:** graphics are drawn from the user's viewpoint.
- **Display:** the combined view is shown to the user.
:::
:::
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Types of AR"}

[Types of Augmented Reality]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-s}
| Type | How Content Is Triggered | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Marker-based | Image, QR code, or fixed pattern is detected | Scanning a printed page to show a 3D model |
| Markerless | Surfaces and motion are tracked using camera and sensors | Placing virtual furniture in a room |
| Location-based | GPS, compass, and map data decide what is shown | Pokemon GO, navigation overlays |
| Projection-based | Light is projected onto real surfaces | Interactive projected keyboards, industrial guidance |
| Superimposition-based | Part of a real object is replaced or enhanced by a digital view | Medical imaging overlay, car-repair guidance |
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="AR Examples"}

[AR in Everyday Use]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- **Camera filters** on social-media applications.
- **Virtual try-on** for glasses, clothes, and cosmetics.
- **Furniture preview:** viewing a sofa in your own room before buying.
- **Navigation:** arrows overlaid on live street view.
- **Translation:** pointing a phone at a sign to see translated text.
- **Games:** Pokemon GO and other location-based games.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="What Is Virtual Reality?"}

[What Is Virtual Reality (VR)?]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
**Virtual Reality** is a technology that creates a **fully computer-generated, three-dimensional environment** with which the user can interact, giving a sense of **being present** inside it.

- The real world is **blocked out or replaced**.
- The user is **immersed** through visual, audio, and sometimes haptic feedback.
- The view **changes with head and body movement**.
- VR is usually experienced with a **head-mounted display (HMD)** and controllers.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Core Concepts of VR"}

[Key Concepts in VR]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- **Immersion:** how strongly the system surrounds the user's senses.
- **Presence:** the feeling of "being there" in the virtual world.
- **Interactivity:** the ability to act on the environment and see responses.
- **Degrees of Freedom (DoF):** 3DoF tracks head rotation; 6DoF also tracks movement through space.
- **Field of View (FoV):** the visible extent of the virtual world.
- **Latency:** the delay between user movement and display update; high latency can cause discomfort.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="VR Architecture"}

[Architecture of a VR System]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    U[User Movement] --> T[Tracking Sensors]
    C[Controllers / Gloves] --> P[Processing Unit]
    T --> P
    W[3D World and Application] --> P
    P --> D[Head-Mounted Display]
    P --> A[Spatial Audio / Haptics]
    D --> U
    A --> U
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.incremental .body-text-m}
- **Input:** tracking and controllers capture user actions.
- **Processing:** a computer, console, or standalone headset runs the application.
- **Output:** display, sound, and touch feedback create immersion.
- **Loop:** every user movement updates the scene in real time.
:::
:::
:::

## {data-menu-title="Hardware Components"}

[Hardware Used in AR and VR]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-s}
| Category | Components | Used In |
|---|---|---|
| Display | Head-mounted display, smart glasses, smartphone or tablet screen | AR and VR |
| Sensors | Camera, gyroscope, accelerometer, depth sensor, GPS | AR and VR |
| Input | Handheld controllers, gloves, hand and eye tracking, voice | AR and VR |
| Processing | CPU, GPU, mobile processor, or a connected PC/console | AR and VR |
| Feedback | Spatial audio, haptic devices, motion platforms | Mostly VR |
| Connectivity | Wi-Fi, 5G, cloud rendering | AR and VR |
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Software Components"}

[Software Used in AR and VR]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- **3D modelling tools** for creating objects and environments.
- **Game and real-time engines** such as Unity and Unreal Engine for building applications.
- **AR frameworks and SDKs** such as ARCore, ARKit, and Vuforia for tracking and scene understanding.
- **Open standards** such as WebXR and OpenXR to run experiences across devices.
- **Computer vision and AI** for recognizing objects, gestures, and surroundings.
- **Cloud services** for storage, rendering, and multi-user experiences.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="AR vs VR"}

[Augmented Reality vs Virtual Reality]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-s}
| Feature | Augmented Reality | Virtual Reality |
|---|---|---|
| Environment | Real world with digital overlay | Fully virtual world |
| Presence | User stays aware of the real surroundings | User is isolated from the real surroundings |
| Typical device | Smartphone, tablet, smart glasses | Head-mounted display with controllers |
| Immersion level | Partial | High |
| Mobility | High; used anywhere | Often limited to a safe play area |
| Main purpose | Enhance real-world tasks | Replace the environment for simulation or experience |
| Examples | Furniture preview, navigation overlay | Flight simulator, VR games, virtual tours |
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Mixed Reality"}

[Mixed Reality (MR)]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- **Mixed Reality** blends real and virtual worlds so that **digital objects can interact with real objects**.
- The system understands the physical space, such as walls, tables, and floors.
- A virtual ball can bounce off a real table; a virtual screen can be pinned to a real wall.
- MR is commonly delivered through advanced headsets with passthrough cameras or transparent lenses.

**Key idea:** AR *adds* content, VR *replaces* the world, and MR *anchors and interacts* with the world.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Features"}

[Key Features of AR and VR]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- **Interactivity:** users can act upon and respond to digital content.
- **Real-time operation:** the display updates instantly with user movement.
- **3D visualization:** objects can be viewed from any angle and scale.
- **Immersion and presence:** engaging and memorable experiences.
- **Safe simulation:** risky or costly tasks can be practiced without real danger.
- **Personalization:** content can adapt to user needs, location, and context.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Applications I"}

[Applications: Education, Healthcare, Industry]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-s}
| Area | AR Applications | VR Applications |
|---|---|---|
| Education | 3D models in textbooks, interactive labs | Virtual field trips, virtual classrooms, history recreation |
| Healthcare | Vein visualization, surgical guidance | Surgical training, pain management, therapy for phobias |
| Industry | Assembly and maintenance instructions, remote expert help | Worker safety training, product prototyping |
| Architecture and Construction | Viewing a building plan on site | Virtual walkthrough before construction |
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Applications II"}

[Applications: Business, Defence, Entertainment]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-s}
| Area | AR Applications | VR Applications |
|---|---|---|
| Retail and Marketing | Virtual try-on, product preview | Virtual showrooms and stores |
| Defence and Aviation | Head-up displays, battlefield information | Flight, vehicle, and combat simulators |
| Tourism | Interactive maps and heritage-site information | Virtual tours of distant destinations |
| Entertainment | Location-based games, live-event overlays | Immersive games, films, and concerts |
| Social and Collaboration | Shared annotations on real objects | Virtual meetings and shared worlds |
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Benefits"}

[Advantages of AR and VR]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- Improves **understanding** through visual and experiential learning.
- Provides **safe training** for dangerous or expensive tasks.
- Reduces **cost** of physical prototypes and travel.
- Increases **engagement** and retention.
- Supports **remote collaboration** and expert assistance.
- Improves **accessibility** by letting people experience places they cannot physically visit.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Limitations"}

[Limitations and Challenges]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- **Cost:** quality headsets, sensors, and powerful computers can be expensive.
- **Health effects:** motion sickness, eye strain, fatigue, and dizziness (often called cybersickness).
- **Hardware limits:** bulky devices, short battery life, limited field of view.
- **Content creation:** developing quality 3D content needs time and skill.
- **Tracking errors:** poor lighting or fast motion can break alignment in AR.
- **Connectivity:** cloud-based and multi-user experiences need fast networks.
- **Safety:** users may collide with real objects or lose awareness of their surroundings.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Ethical Issues"}

[Privacy, Security, and Ethical Concerns]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- Cameras and sensors may capture **personal spaces, faces, and behaviour**.
- Eye-tracking, movement, and biometric data can reveal **sensitive information**.
- **Content distraction** while driving or walking can cause accidents.
- **Addiction and escapism** may arise from prolonged use of immersive worlds.
- **Digital divide:** costly devices may increase inequality of access.
- Responsible design needs **consent, data protection, and age-appropriate use**.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Case Study"}

[Case Study: Training a Surgeon with VR and AR]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- **Before surgery (VR):** the trainee practices a procedure on a virtual patient as many times as needed, without risk.
- **During planning (VR/AR):** scans such as CT and MRI are turned into a 3D model that can be rotated and examined.
- **During surgery (AR):** key information or anatomy can be overlaid on the surgeon's view.
- **After training:** the system records performance for feedback.

**Lesson:** VR gives a safe practice space, while AR supports real-world tasks with timely information.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Future Trends"}

[Future Trends]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- Lighter, cheaper, and **wireless standalone** headsets.
- **AR smart glasses** that may gradually replace some phone use.
- Integration with **AI** for object recognition, assistants, and content generation.
- **5G and edge computing** for low-latency cloud rendering.
- **Digital twins and the metaverse** for shared virtual spaces.
- Better **haptics and eye/hand tracking** for natural interaction.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Key Concepts"}

[Important Definitions and Key Terminology]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-s}
- **AR:** Augmented Reality; digital content overlaid on the real world.
- **VR:** Virtual Reality; fully computer-generated immersive environment.
- **MR:** Mixed Reality; real and virtual objects interact.
- **XR:** Extended Reality; umbrella term for AR, VR, and MR.
- **HMD:** Head-Mounted Display.
- **Immersion:** degree to which the system engages the user's senses.
- **Presence:** feeling of being inside the virtual environment.
- **DoF:** Degrees of Freedom of tracked movement.
- **Latency:** delay between user action and system response.
- **Registration:** alignment of virtual content with the real world.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Summary"}

[Lecture Summary]{.slide-title}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- AR overlays digital content on the real world; VR replaces the real world with a virtual one.
- MR lets real and virtual objects interact; XR covers AR, VR, and MR.
- AR works through capture, tracking, registration, rendering, and display.
- VR depends on tracking, processing, and display with low latency for immersion and presence.
- Both technologies are used in education, healthcare, industry, defence, retail, tourism, and entertainment.
- Cost, health effects, hardware limits, content creation, and privacy are major challenges.
:::

## {data-menu-title="Knowledge Check"}

[Knowledge Check: MCQs]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-s}
1. Which technology overlays digital content on the real-world view?  
   A. Virtual Reality  B. Augmented Reality  C. Grid Computing  D. Green Computing  
   **Answer: B**

2. Which device is most commonly used for full VR immersion?  
   A. Barcode reader  B. Scanner  C. Head-mounted display  D. Printer  
   **Answer: C**

3. The delay between user movement and display update in VR is called:  
   A. Bandwidth  B. Latency  C. Resolution  D. Registration  
   **Answer: B**

4. Placing virtual furniture in your room using a phone camera is an example of:  
   A. VR  B. AR  C. Cloud storage  D. Blockchain  
   **Answer: B**
:::
